title: Plant faults in the forms writers produce
statement: Plant each check's test faults in the forms writers actually produce, not only the blatant one, since a check that catches its planted form can pass every other.
example: A line-number check tested only on digits passed 13 lines in three ready blocks that pointed by position in words, such as 'the tenth line'.
detail: The lesson engine's house check for line numbers matches only 'L' or 'line' followed by digits, and its test plants only digit forms such as 'line 12'. On a poem and a speech the writer kept to the letter of the rule and pointed by position in words instead, such as 'the sixth line', 'the opening line' and 'the first sentence': 13 such lines passed in three ready blocks, 5 of them in what a student is shown. The check that a wrong option's feedback doesn't name the answer has one planted fault, which writes a whole right option of several words into the feedback, so nothing showed that it needs a shared run of at least three words and can never fire on a key of one or two words; a film block's feedback saying the play was written 'around 1603', for the key 'Around 1603', passed.

evidence.quote: Text a student reads never cites a line number (no "L12",
assert.equal(houseChecks({ feedback: ["Look again at line 12."] })[0].ok, false);
Re-read the sixth line to see what spiritual quality the speaker says cannot be bestowed by speeches alone.
Re-read the tenth line to consider the permanent claim of power in the title.
Listen again to hear that the play was written around 1603.
